title: Chemical Composition of Juniperus sabina L. Essential Oil from Mongolia and Its Preliminary Radical-Scavenging and Anti-Neuroinflammatory Activity in Cell Models
content: Juniperus sabina L. is a medicinal plant with reported antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, but its essential oil has been little studied in Mongolian plant material, and its anti-neuroinflammatory potential remains largely unexplored. The primary aim of this study was to characterize the chemical composition of J. sabina essential oil (JSEO) from Mongolia; its radical-scavenging activity, cytotoxicity and effects on inflammatory responses in microglial cells were then examined in a preliminary screening. The essential oil was extracted by hydrodistillation and analyzed using gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS). Radical-scavenging activity was assessed using the DPPH assay, while cytotoxicity was evaluated in Neuro-2a neuroblastoma and BV-2 microglial cells using the MTT assay. The effects of JSEO on lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced nitric oxide (NO) production and cytokine secretion were investigated in BV-2 cells. Forty-six compounds were tentatively identified, with sabinene being the predominant constituent (25.81%). JSEO exhibited very weak DPPH radical-scavenging activity, with an IC₅₀ of 25,256 ± 5478 µg/mL compared with 2.96 ± 0.12 µg/mL for Trolox. Relative to an LPS-stimulated vehicle control, JSEO lowered nitrite accumulation by approximately 21% and 53% at 100 and 200 µg/mL without reducing cell viability, whereas the apparent effect at 50 µg/mL was attributable to the vehicle alone. At 200 µg/mL, JSEO also lowered IL-6 and TNF-α secretion by approximately 76% and 43%, respectively, whereas IL-10 was below the lower limit of quantification in all samples. This study provides the first compositional description of JSEO from Uvurkhangai province, Mongolia. The cell-based measurements were made on three technical replicate wells within a single experiment and are reported descriptively without statistical testing; they suggest that JSEO may modulate inflammatory responses in activated microglial cells despite its weak direct radical-scavenging activity, a possibility that now requires confirmation in independently repeated experiments.
